ALL.text:
Allstate's #5 ranking is driven almost entirely by Value and Growth, with Quality lagging well behind. The Value score of 93 reflects a P/E of just 6.4 and P/FCF of 6.66 — multiples that look inexpensive even for an insurer, alongside a P/B of 2.15 that's reasonable given a 33.59% ROE. The Growth score of 96.6 is powered by the eye-catching 101.73% revenue growth figure. Momentum at 57.9 is middling, suggesting the stock hasn't been chased higher the way the cheap valuation and growth numbers might imply, which is worth noting as a lack of confirming price action. Quality at 47.7 is the drag, and it's largely a data-quality issue as much as a business one: ROIC, gross/operating margins, debt/EBITDA, Altman Z-Score, and Piotroski F-Score are all marked n/a, likely reflecting how insurance company financials don't map cleanly onto standard non-financial templates (premiums, claims reserves, and underwriting income don't translate into "gross margin" the way they do for a retailer or manufacturer).

The bigger thing to double-check is that 101.73% revenue growth number — for a mature, large insurer like Allstate, that magnitude is unusual and may reflect a one-off accounting item, a prior-year base distortion (e.g., catastrophe losses or reserve charges depressing the year-ago figure), or a change in how premium revenue is recognized, rather than genuine underlying business expansion. Given that Growth contributes 20% of the score and is the single largest percentile after Value, a reader should verify this figure against Allstate's actual filings before weighting it heavily. Low leverage (debt/equity 0.24) is a genuine positive supporting the Quality/Value combination even where other Quality metrics are blank.

GOOG.text:
Alphabet's #32 ranking and 56.7 final score are built on three fairly strong factors — Growth (72.3), Quality (66.5) and Momentum (66.4) — dragged down by a weak Value score (22.7). The Growth reading is supported by 15.1% year-over-year revenue growth and a punchier 34.2% EPS growth, suggesting margin expansion and share buybacks are amplifying bottom-line gains beyond top-line pace. Quality is anchored by genuinely elite profitability: 31.8% ROE, 27.7% ROIC, a 59.7% gross margin and roughly 32% operating and net margins. The balance sheet reinforces this — Debt/Equity of just 0.12, a 2.01 current ratio, and an extraordinarily high Altman Z-Score of 16.28 point to minimal financial-distress risk. Momentum in the mid-60s indicates the stock has been performing well relative to peers.

The obvious tension is valuation. A P/E of 31.6, P/B of 10.05, P/S of 10.36 and especially P/FCF near 57 explain the depressed 22.7 Value score — buyers are paying a premium, and the model flags little margin of safety. Worth double-checking: FCF growth was essentially flat at 0.69%, a sharp divergence from the 34% EPS growth, which may reflect heavy capital expenditure (likely AI/data-center spending) consuming cash. The Piotroski F-Score of 6/9 is solid but not pristine, hinting at some softness beneath the headline profitability. Finally, with Momentum already elevated, readers should consider how much good news is already reflected in the price, and whether the stretched P/FCF leaves room for disappointment.

ANET.text:
Arista Networks lands at #24 with a final score of 54.4, a result of strong quality, growth, and momentum being almost entirely offset by an extremely weak value score of 6.9. The quality picture is solid: 28.4% ROE, 64% gross margin, and a 42.8% operating margin point to a business with real pricing power and operating leverage, likely tied to its position in high-end networking hardware for cloud and AI data centers. Growth of 70.5 is backed by 24% revenue growth and 23% EPS growth, both healthy for a company of this size ($251B market cap), and momentum at 72.5 suggests the market has been rewarding this performance with a rising share price. The Altman Z-Score of 23.74 signals essentially no bankruptcy risk, and a current ratio above 3 shows ample short-term liquidity.

The glaring outlier is valuation. A P/E of 89, P/S near 28, and P/B above 20 put ANET in rarefied territory — the market is pricing in years of continued 20%+ growth and margin durability. That's the main thing to double-check: at these multiples, even a modest deceleration in cloud/AI-related networking demand could trigger a sharp re-rating, since so little room for disappointment is priced in. The Piotroski F-Score of 5/9, middling rather than strong, hints that not every fundamental trend (working capital, margins, leverage trajectory) is moving in the ideal direction simultaneously. Debt/EBITDA and ROIC are both unavailable, which limits how thoroughly capital efficiency and leverage can be verified here — worth checking directly in filings before relying on the quality score alone. Momentum being this high after a large run also raises the question of how much good news is already reflected in the price.

CFG.text:
Citizens Financial Group's mid-pack score of 51.6 reflects a lopsided factor profile: cheap valuation offset by weak profitability. The Value score of 76.2 stands out, with a P/E of 17.61, P/B of just 1.1, and P/FCF of 13.13 — all suggesting the market is pricing the bank modestly relative to earnings and book value, typical of regional banks trading below their larger peers. Momentum at 54 is unremarkable, neither a tailwind nor a drag. But Quality sits at just 36.5, driven by an ROE of only 6.96%, which is thin for a bank and signals the company is not generating strong returns on shareholder capital relative to peers. Growth at 40.7 is similarly soft, with revenue essentially flat year-over-year (0.14%), even though EPS jumped 26.24% — a gap that suggests earnings gains came from cost control, buybacks, or lower provisions rather than core business expansion.

A reader should note the perfect Piotroski F-Score of 9/9, which does indicate improving fundamentals (better margins, leverage, and efficiency trends) even if the absolute profitability level remains low. Debt/Equity of 0.43 looks conservative, but for a bank, standard leverage and credit-quality metrics like Debt/EBITDA, current ratio, and Altman Z-Score are marked "n/a" — these simply don't translate well to financial institutions, so they shouldn't be read as red flags, but it also means the model has less visibility into balance-sheet risk here than for a typical industrial company. The disconnect between strong EPS growth and flat revenue is worth double-checking before weighting the growth figure too heavily.

LLY.text:
Eli Lilly lands at #14 with a final score of 59.7, powered almost entirely by growth and momentum rather than valuation. Growth sits at 88.7, reflecting genuinely explosive fundamentals: revenue up 38.2% year-over-year, EPS up 95.6%, and free cash flow up 90.7%, driven largely by demand for its GLP-1 drugs. Momentum at 78.7 confirms the market has been rewarding this with sustained price strength. Quality at 67.9 is solid but not exceptional given the underlying numbers — ROE of 77.8% and a Piotroski F-Score of 8/9 point to strong fundamental health and efficient capital use, though gross margin of 83% paired with an unavailable operating margin figure makes it hard to fully verify how much of that profitability survives past cost of goods sold. The real drag is Value at just 7.7, among the weakest in the ranked universe — a P/E of 85, P/B of 39, and P/S of nearly 16 signal the stock is priced for years of continued outperformance.

What this hides is the risk embedded in that valuation gap. A stock growing this fast and trading at this multiple leaves little room for disappointment; any deceleration in GLP-1 demand, pricing pressure, or competitive entrants could compress the premium sharply. Debt/Equity of 1.6 is worth watching too, even though the current ratio of 1.58 suggests near-term liquidity is fine — leverage combined with a missing Debt/EBITDA figure makes it harder to gauge balance-sheet cushion. Momentum this strong, this late in a multi-year run, also means much of the good news may already be priced in.

ADI.text:
Analog Devices lands at #16 with a final score of 53.4, and the ranking is clearly powered by its Momentum (83.6) and Growth (77.9) factors. The growth story is concrete: revenue is up 29.75% year-over-year, EPS has jumped 83.19%, and free cash flow grew 37%, with a recent 5.33% earnings surprise reinforcing the upward trend. The business itself shows genuine quality in its margin structure — a 64.49% gross margin, 32.5% operating margin, and 26.01% net margin are strong for a semiconductor company — and a Piotroski F-Score of 8/9 signals healthy fundamental momentum. Leverage is modest, with debt/equity at 0.26 and a current ratio of 1.75.

The tension lies in the two weaker factors. Value scores just 19.3, and the multiples explain why: a P/E of 58, P/S of 15.13, P/B of 5.74, and P/FCF of 42 all price ADI as an expensive stock. Quality is only middling at 40.3 despite those fat margins, because returns on capital are thin — ROE of 9.79% and ROIC of 7.79% are unremarkable, and gross profit/assets of 14.1% suggests a heavy, capital-intensive balance sheet.

A reader should weigh a few things. The eye-catching EPS and revenue growth likely reflect recovery off a cyclical trough, so those rates may not be sustainable — semiconductor demand is notoriously cyclical. High momentum can also arrive late in a run. And a rich valuation leaves little cushion if growth decelerates or ROIC stays subdued relative to the price being paid.

TER.text:
Teradyne's #9 ranking is overwhelmingly a momentum story, with a near-top-decile momentum score of 96.7 doing most of the heavy lifting. That's backed by real fundamental strength: revenue grew 30.3% year-over-year, EPS jumped 52.9%, and the latest earnings surprise of 20.5% suggests the business is beating expectations as the semiconductor test cycle turns. Quality is solid at 59.3, supported by a 29.7% ROE, 28.7% ROIC, and healthy margins (58.7% gross, 26.5% operating). The balance sheet is pristine — essentially zero debt, a 2.15 current ratio, and an Altman Z-Score of 26.1 that signals virtually no bankruptcy risk. Growth at 66.8 rounds out a picture of a profitable, expanding, financially sound company.

The glaring weakness is Value, scoring just 4.7 — near the bottom of the universe. Investors are paying a steep price for that growth and momentum: a P/E of 65.9, P/B of 13.76, P/S of 14.87, and a P/FCF above 100. Those multiples leave little margin for error if growth decelerates.

A reader should double-check a few tensions. First, the momentum score is very high, which often comes late in a run and can reverse sharply in cyclical semiconductor names. Second, despite strong EPS growth, free cash flow actually fell 5%, and the Piotroski F-Score of 6/9 is only moderate — worth reconciling against the rosy income-statement figures. Finally, the rich valuation means much of the good news may already be priced in.

PNC.text:
PNC's #17 ranking and 53.4 composite are anchored by its Value factor (73.4), the standout among its four scores. On the surface the valuation is undemanding: a P/E of 14.0, P/B of 1.31, and P/FCF of 14.8 are modest for a large-cap bank, and a 28.83% net margin alongside a 34.54% operating margin reflects the typically high-margin economics of a diversified financial institution. Growth (55.2) and Momentum (51.1) both sit near the middle of the pack, so the stock is neither leading nor lagging on price trend, while reported revenue growth of 72.27% is eye-catching and helps the Growth reading.

The clear drag is Quality at 37.6, the weakest factor and a meaningful counterweight given Quality carries the largest weight in the model. ROE of 11.98% and ROIC of just 6.89% are unremarkable, and the Debt/Equity of 0.71 reflects the leverage inherent to a bank's balance sheet — worth noting that many quality sub-metrics (Altman Z, Piotroski, current ratio, gross margin) read "n/a," which is normal for financials but means the Quality score rests on a thinner set of inputs.

A reader should scrutinize the growth figures: 72.27% revenue growth is unusually large and likely reflects accounting or comparison-base quirks common in bank revenue, not sustainable organic expansion. It also sits against a -44.4% decline in free cash flow, a divergence worth understanding. The near-flat 0.84% earnings surprise suggests results are landing broadly in line with expectations rather than accelerating.

PFG.text:
Principal Financial's rank of #15 reflects a mixed but interesting profile. Value and Momentum are the standout drivers, at 80.4 and 79.2 respectively. The value case rests on a P/E of 23.27 and P/B of 2.21 that look unremarkable at first glance, but the P/FCF of 5.78 stands out as genuinely cheap relative to the market, suggesting the stock generates substantial free cash flow relative to its price — a common trait among insurers with large, low-capex balance sheets. Momentum near the 80th percentile indicates the stock has been outperforming peers recently, which combined with a still-modest P/E suggests the market hasn't fully re-rated the stock despite the run. Quality (43.5) and Growth (30.1) are the drags: ROE under 10% is middling for a financial, and EPS growth of -21.45% year-over-year is a real red flag sitting underneath a decent revenue growth figure of 6.93%, implying margin compression, one-off charges, or reserve/investment-related noise rather than a straightforward decline in the core business.

A reader should treat the P/E and EPS growth divergence as the key thing to investigate — a 23x multiple on shrinking earnings is a different story than 23x on stable ones, and it's worth checking whether the EPS drop is tied to actuarial assumptions, realized investment losses, or genuine operating deterioration. The lack of ROIC, margin, and Altman Z-Score data (typical for insurers, where standard operating-margin metrics don't apply cleanly) means quality here is harder to verify than the score implies, and the strong P/FCF figure should be checked against how "free cash flow" is defined for an insurance business, since it can behave very differently than for a typical industrial company.

TROW.text:
T. Rowe Price lands at #28 largely on the strength of its Value score (80.8), which reflects a P/E of 11.5, P/B of 2.11, and P/FCF near 15.5 — multiples that are low relative to the broader market and even to many asset managers, suggesting the market is pricing in limited growth or ongoing pressure on the business. Profitability metrics support the idea that this isn't a low-quality discount: operating margin near 30% and net margin of 28.5% indicate a business that still converts revenue efficiently into profit, and ROE of 19.2% is solid for an asset-light financial firm. However, Quality only scores 51 (middling), and Momentum is weak at 33, meaning the stock has underperformed peers recently in price terms, likely tied to concerns about active-management fee compression and net outflows common in the traditional asset-management industry.

What the numbers may be hiding: Growth is soft at 42.8, with EPS growth essentially flat (0.65% yoy) despite revenue growth of 6.41% — a gap worth checking, since it implies margin compression or rising costs are eating into the topline gain. FCF growth of 17.19% is a brighter spot and could indicate improving cash conversion, but the lack of data on debt levels, current ratio, Altman Z-score, and Piotroski F-score means leverage and balance-sheet resilience can't be verified from this profile alone. Investors should also weigh that AUM-based revenue is sensitive to market swings, so the cheap valuation may partly reflect structural fee and flow risks rather than a temporary mispricing.

MU.text:
Micron's #5 ranking is powered almost entirely by its Momentum (100) and Growth (98.7) scores, both sitting at or near the top of the ranked universe. The growth figures are extraordinary: revenue up 167% year-over-year, EPS up roughly 700%, and free cash flow up over 1,278%, alongside a 17.3% earnings surprise. Quality is also strong at 74.7, supported by a 70.6% ROE, 61.5% ROIC, and margins that are exceptional for a hardware business — 72.6% gross, 65.6% operating, and 55.9% net. The balance sheet reinforces this: debt/equity of just 0.06, debt/EBITDA of 0.8, a current ratio of 3.42, an Altman Z-Score of 25, and a Piotroski F-Score of 8/9. Value is the clear laggard at 34.4, and a large insider-selling penalty (-15) is the single biggest drag on the final 60.8.

A reader should weigh a few things. Momentum pinned at exactly 100 means the stock is at the top of its run, so the score reflects how far it has already moved, not where it goes next. The growth rates are lapping unusually depressed prior-year comparisons — triple-digit expansion is unlikely to repeat, and future quarters will face far tougher year-over-year math. Valuation multiples (P/B 10.3, P/S 12.3, P/FCF 42) already embed rich expectations, explaining the weak Value score. Finally, the heavy insider selling against this backdrop is worth investigating directly, as it partly offsets the otherwise strong quality and growth signals.

HST.text:
Host Hotels & Resorts lands at #21 with a final score of 58.2, driven primarily by its Momentum (80.6) and Value (70.6) percentiles. On the value side, the numbers look reasonable for a REIT: a P/FCF of 10.62 and P/S of 2.62 suggest the stock isn't richly priced relative to cash generation, while the P/E of 20.96 and P/B of 2.44 are more middling. The strong momentum score indicates the shares have been performing well recently. Balance-sheet health is a standout — Debt/Equity of 0.19 and Debt/EBITDA of 0.77 are conservative for a property company, and the Piotroski F-Score of 8/9 signals broadly improving fundamentals. Growth is moderate (48.3), with revenue up 7.57% and EPS up 11.45% year-over-year, though FCF growth is essentially flat at 0.8%.

The weak link is Quality at 35.9. ROE of 11.67% and ROIC of 10.92% are only adequate, and net margin of 12.51% is thin enough that returns aren't distinguishing the business from peers. Several metrics are unavailable (gross margin, current ratio, Altman Z), typical for a REIT, so the model is working with a partial picture.

A reader should note the tension between high momentum and mediocre quality — an 80.6 momentum score late in a run can reverse quickly if hotel demand softens. The near-zero FCF growth also sits awkwardly against the healthier EPS figure, worth checking against occupancy trends, RevPAR, and how the low leverage might change if acquisitions ramp up.

INCY.text:
Incyte's #4 ranking is driven almost entirely by Growth and Momentum, with Quality providing solid support underneath. The Growth score of 90 reflects genuinely strong operating performance: 17.95% revenue growth alongside a much larger jump in reported EPS (4085%) and FCF (321%), suggesting the company has moved decisively past a period of heavy investment or one-off charges and is now converting sales into profit far more efficiently. Momentum at 82 shows the market has already started pricing this shift in. Quality at 72.4 is backed by real fundamentals — 92.76% gross margin, 29.46% operating margin, a Piotroski F-Score of 8/9, an Altman Z-Score above 10 (minimal bankruptcy risk), and a current ratio of 3.32 indicating ample liquidity with no meaningful debt burden. Value sits at a neutral 50, with a P/E of 38 and P/S near 4.76 pricing in continued growth rather than offering a discount.

A few things worth double-checking before taking the growth figures at face value. EPS growth of over 4000% and FCF growth over 300% are almost certainly measured off a depressed prior-year base — possibly a licensing charge, impairment, or unusually low earnings quarter — so the percentage itself overstates the durability of the improvement; the 17.95% revenue growth is a more reliable read on underlying demand. Momentum scores this high also raise the question of how much good news is already reflected in the price, given the P/E of 38 versus P/FCF of 17, a gap that hints the stock trades richer on reported earnings than on cash generation. Finally, ROIC and debt metrics are listed as not available, so leverage and capital efficiency can't be fully verified from these figures alone.

FFIV.text:
F5's overall score of 52 reflects a company with solid but unspectacular fundamentals trading at a rich valuation. Momentum (62.9) is the standout factor, suggesting the stock has been performing well relative to peers recently, which aligns with a strong Piotroski F-Score of 8/9 — a signal that the underlying financial trends (profitability, leverage, efficiency) are improving. Quality (57.9) is respectable, backed by high gross margins (81.4%), a healthy operating margin near 25%, and net margins above 22%, all indicative of F5's software/security-driven business model with real pricing power. Growth (55.5) is middling: revenue growth of just 4.77% is modest for a tech name, though EPS growth of nearly 24% and FCF growth of almost 19% show that profitability is expanding faster than the top line, likely through margin discipline or buybacks.

The clear laggard is Value (31.2), and this is where a reader should look closely. A P/E of 45.4, P/B of nearly 7, and P/S above 8 are elevated multiples for a company growing revenue in the mid-single digits. The gap between strong EPS/FCF growth and weak revenue growth raises the question of how repeatable that earnings acceleration is — if it's driven by one-time cost cuts or buybacks rather than durable demand, the current valuation offers less cushion. Also worth noting: ROIC, debt/equity, debt/EBITDA, and Altman Z-Score are all listed as unavailable, so the leverage and credit-risk picture is incomplete here, and investors should verify balance-sheet risk independently rather than relying on the model's quality score alone.

CINF.text:
Cincinnati Financial's ranking is anchored by a striking Value score of 88.3, reflecting a P/E of just 12.12, P/B of 1.66, and P/FCF of 8.53 — cheap multiples for an insurer generating a 15% ROE and 18.95% net margin. The balance sheet is essentially unlevered (Debt/Equity of 0.05), which is typical for a conservatively run property-casualty insurer and reduces financial risk. Growth is middling-positive at 55.6, supported by 12.3% revenue growth and 17.7% FCF growth, though EPS growth lagged at just 4.6%, suggesting some margin or underwriting drag between top-line gains and bottom-line profit. Quality sits at a mediocre 52.9, with a Piotroski score of 6/9 indicating reasonably sound fundamentals but not best-in-class. The standout weak spot is Momentum at 22.3 — the stock has lagged peers in price performance recently, which is the main factor holding the composite score down to 54.6 and the rank to #23.

A few things worth double-checking: many standard profitability and leverage metrics (ROIC, gross/operating margin, Debt/EBITDA, current ratio, Altman Z-Score) are marked "n/a," which is common for insurers whose financial statements don't map cleanly onto industry-agnostic templates — this means the Quality and Value scores are being computed on a thinner metric set than for a typical company, so the cheapness signal should be viewed with some caution rather than taken as directly comparable across sectors. The gap between EPS growth (4.6%) and revenue/FCF growth (12–18%) is also worth investigating, as it could reflect rising combined ratios, catastrophe losses, or reserve strengthening — normal for P&C insurers but relevant to understanding why earnings aren't keeping pace with premium growth. Finally, the weak momentum score alongside cheap valuation could mean the market is pricing in underwriting or investment-portfolio concerns not fully captured in these backward-looking metrics.

NTAP.text:
NetApp's rank of #10 is driven almost entirely by momentum, which at 93.8 sits near the top of the ranked universe, alongside a solid quality score of 74.5. The momentum reading reflects strong recent price action, but with growth at just 37.7 and revenue actually contracting slightly (-0.25% year-over-year), the market appears to be rewarding execution and capital efficiency rather than top-line expansion. That efficiency shows up clearly in the quality metrics: ROE of 94.45% and ROIC of 73.31% are exceptional, operating margin near 27%, and a Piotroski F-Score of 7/9 signals healthy balance-sheet and profitability trends. EPS growth of 10.29% and FCF growth of nearly 40% suggest the company is expanding profitability and cash generation even as revenue stays flat, likely through margin discipline, buybacks, or mix shift.

The value score of 41.2 is middling, and the valuation multiples explain why — a P/E of 34, P/B of 29, and P/S over 6 are rich for a company with no revenue growth this year. Much of the ROE figure is also inflated by leverage and a thin equity base: debt/equity of 1.84 means returns are partly a function of balance-sheet structure rather than pure operating strength, so ROE alone shouldn't be read as a clean quality signal. Investors should also note that the momentum score is a trailing measure — a 93.8 percentile ranking this high often means the stock has already made a large move, and readers should check how much of that move has already priced in the FCF growth and margin improvement before assuming it continues. With flat revenue, growth durability is the key open question.

STT.text:
State Street's #3 ranking is driven overwhelmingly by momentum, which at 93.8 sits near the top of the entire ranked universe, alongside a strong value score of 80.6. The momentum reading suggests the stock has been on a sustained, powerful price run, likely reflecting improving sentiment toward custody banks and trust institutions as rates and market activity have supported fee income. Value support comes from a P/E of 20.61 and a strikingly low P/FCF of 4.8, the latter turbocharged by FCF growth of 176.7% year-over-year — a number that flatters the ratio but may not be repeatable. Growth at 62.8 is respectable, backed by 8% revenue growth and nearly 15% EPS growth, while quality at 56.9 is middling, consistent with a 10.58% ROE and 21% net margin that are solid but unspectacular for a financial franchise of this scale.

What deserves a closer look: the extreme momentum score means much of the good news may already be priced in, and stocks ranking this high on momentum can be vulnerable to sharp reversals if sentiment shifts. The P/FCF figure should be treated cautiously given the outsized 176.7% growth rate behind it — a base-year distortion (low prior-year FCF) could be inflating the apparent cheapness rather than reflecting a durable cash-generation improvement. Also notable is the absence of standard balance-sheet and quality metrics — Debt/Equity, Debt/EBITDA, current ratio, Altman Z-Score, and Piotroski F-Score are all unavailable, which is typical for a bank holding company but means leverage and balance-sheet risk simply aren't visible in this factor model and would need separate scrutiny of the balance sheet and capital ratios.

USB.text:
U.S. Bancorp's mid-pack rank of #34 with a 51.6 score reflects a split profile: a cheap valuation offset by mediocre quality and weak growth. The Value factor at 80.7 is the clear standout — a P/E of 14.5, P/B of 1.43, and P/FCF under 12 suggest the market is pricing this regional bank at a discount relative to peers, and a Piotroski F-Score of 8/9 indicates solid underlying fundamental trends (improving profitability, leverage, and efficiency signals) that support the value case. Momentum is roughly neutral at 48.3, meaning the stock isn't being rewarded or punished much by the market currently. Quality (44.5) and Growth (30.2) are the drags: ROE of 11.6% is unremarkable for a bank, and revenue growth of just 0.91% year-over-year shows the top line is essentially stagnant, which is typical for large regional banks in a slow-loan-growth environment.

A reader should note a few gaps in the data that make this harder to fully evaluate. ROIC, Debt/EBITDA, and Altman Z-Score are all n/a, again largely because these metrics aren't well-suited to a lender's balance sheet — a reader should instead look at capital ratios, net interest margin, and loan-loss provisions (not shown here) to judge quality. Also worth flagging: FCF fell 29.3% year-over-year despite EPS growth of 20.4%, a divergence that's worth understanding before leaning too heavily on the low P/FCF multiple as a sign of cheapness.

MTB.text:
M&T Bank lands at #35 with a final score of 55.3, and its most influential driver is Value at 69.4. That reading is supported by a P/E of 13.39, a P/B of 1.31, and a P/FCF of 12.71 — modest multiples typical of a regional bank and cheaper than much of the broader market. The standout underlying signal is a perfect Piotroski F-Score of 9/9, which points to broad-based improvement in profitability, leverage, and operating efficiency and helps explain why Quality holds up at 53 despite a fairly ordinary ROE of 9.77%. EPS growth of 16.17% year-over-year outpaces revenue growth of 7.53%, suggesting margin or efficiency gains rather than pure top-line expansion. Momentum (51.5) and Growth (45.9) are middling, so this profile leans on being reasonably priced and fundamentally clean rather than fast-growing or trending.

A few figures warrant a closer look. Several bank-specific metrics — gross/operating margin, ROIC, current ratio, Altman Z — read "n/a," which is normal for financials but means the model is working with a thinner data set here. The reported net margin of 172% and P/S of 23 are artifacts of how bank revenue is measured and should not be taken at face value. FCF growth of -16.81% pulls against the otherwise improving picture and is worth reconciling against that 9/9 F-Score. Finally, ROE below 10% is unremarkable for the sector, so the Value score reflects a cheap stock more than an exceptional franchise — verify how rates and credit conditions are affecting earnings.

GOOGL.text:
Alphabet lands at #31 with a final score of 56.7, and its ranking is built on a fairly balanced spread across three of the four factors. Growth (72.3) is the standout, supported by 15.1% year-over-year revenue growth and a stronger 34.2% jump in EPS, suggesting operating leverage and margin discipline rather than growth bought at any cost. Momentum (68.9) and Quality (66.5) reinforce that picture: net margin of 32.8%, operating margin of 32.0%, ROE of 31.8% and ROIC of 27.7% describe a highly profitable business, while a debt/equity of just 0.12, a current ratio of 2.0 and an Altman Z-Score of 16.4 point to a fortress balance sheet with minimal solvency risk.

The clear drag is Value at 20.4 — a bottom-quintile score. At a P/E of 31.9, P/B of 10.2, P/S of 10.5 and a notably steep P/FCF of 57.6, the market is pricing in continued strong execution, so much of the quality and growth is already reflected in the price.

A few things worth checking behind the composite. The P/FCF gap versus the P/E hints at heavy capital spending, and indeed FCF growth was flat at just 0.69% despite 34% EPS growth — worth understanding whether that reflects AI/data-center investment or weakening cash conversion. The Piotroski score of 6/9 is solid but not pristine. Finally, elevated momentum this late in a large-cap run and a $4.2T market cap mean expectations are high, leaving less cushion if growth decelerates.

FDX.text:
FedEx's ranking at #35 (51.4/100) is a story of cheapness colliding with weak quality signals, netting out to a middling score. Value is the standout at 81.5 — a P/E of 16.79, P/S of 0.76, and P/FCF of 14.07 all point to a stock trading at a discount relative to the broader market, consistent with FedEx's mature, capital-intensive, low-margin logistics business. Momentum at 62.3 suggests the stock has had a decent run recently, and Growth of 48.8 is roughly average, supported by 10.16% EPS growth and a striking 71.62% jump in free cash flow, even though top-line revenue growth is a modest 3.93%. The problem is Quality, scoring just 18.9. An operating margin of 5.77% and net margin of 4.68% are thin for a company this size, ROIC of 9.83% is unremarkable, and a Piotroski F-Score of 6/9 is only middling on fundamental health.

What's worth double-checking: the FCF growth figure of 71.62% is likely flattering a low or volatile prior-year base (capex timing, asset sales, or working-capital swings), so it shouldn't be read as a durable trend without looking at multi-year FCF history. Debt/EBITDA of 2.46 and Debt/Equity of 0.76 aren't alarming, but combined with thin margins they mean there's less cushion if freight volumes or pricing soften. Gross margin and Altman Z-Score are both listed as "n/a," so leverage and margin-of-safety metrics that analysts typically lean on for a cyclical, asset-heavy business are effectively missing from this view — worth sourcing elsewhere before weighing the value case too heavily.

PFS.text:
Provident Financial's #9 ranking (65.8/100) is anchored by its Value score of 84.7, the strongest of its four factors. The valuation metrics support this: a P/E of 10.0, price-to-book of 0.96 (trading just below stated book value), and a P/FCF of 7.23 all point to a modestly priced regional bank. Growth is also a meaningful contributor at 70.6, reflecting reported revenue growth of 36.7% and EPS growth of 111.8% year-over-year, alongside a nearly 10% earnings surprise. Quality lands mid-pack at 60.2, with a 30.2% net margin and 40.9% operating margin that are typical for a bank, ROE just under 11%, ROIC of 9.3%, and low debt/equity of 0.18. Momentum is the weakest link at 49.9, essentially neutral, suggesting the market has not rewarded the stock much despite the strong fundamentals.

A reader should treat the eye-catching growth figures with caution. Triple-digit EPS growth and 36.7% revenue growth are unusually large for an established bank and often reflect merger-related activity, one-off items, or an easy prior-year comparison rather than organic expansion — worth checking against the actual earnings history. Note also that FCF growth was just 1.3%, a stark contrast to the headline EPS number. Many standard quality and safety metrics (Piotroski, Altman Z, gross margin, current ratio) are not applicable to banks, so the Quality score rests on a narrower base. Finally, a sub-book valuation can signal either value or market skepticism about asset quality and net interest margin pressure.

SGHC.text:
SGHC lands at #22 with a 56.5 composite, and the profile is tilted toward Growth (71.6) and Quality (66.1) rather than Value. The Growth score is backed by real momentum in the underlying business: revenue grew nearly 20% year-over-year and EPS jumped 79.8%, suggesting operating leverage is flowing through as the top line scales. Quality is supported by an unusually strong return profile — ROE of 33.5% and ROIC of 30.1% — alongside a very light balance sheet, with Debt/Equity of just 0.14 and a current ratio of 1.61. Momentum at 62.7 rounds out a broadly constructive picture, while Value (26.8) is the clear laggard.

The tension here is valuation. A P/E of 30.75, P/B of 7.53 and P/S of 3.25 mean investors are already paying up for the growth and returns, which is why the Value factor drags against the other three. That premium leaves less room for error, and the latest earnings surprise came in at –3.88% — a modest miss worth watching against the priced-in expectations.

A few blanks deserve scrutiny: gross margin, Debt/EBITDA, Altman Z and Piotroski scores are all "n/a," so the quality read leans heavily on ROE and ROIC without the usual balance-sheet stress checks. Net margin of 10.58% is healthy but thinner than the operating margin of 16.81% suggests, hinting at meaningful below-the-line costs. Readers should confirm whether the triple-digit EPS growth is sustainable operating improvement or partly one-off effects.

SU.text:
Suncor's #34 rank and 53/100 score are propelled almost entirely by momentum (79.8), the standout factor here. That reflects strong recent price performance and a modest 4.68% earnings surprise. Value sits comfortably above average at 56.1, supported by an undemanding P/E of 15.64 and a P/FCF of 13.69 — reasonable multiples for a large integrated energy producer generating real cash. Quality is middling at 50.3: ROE of 14% and ROIC of 10.6% are respectable but not exceptional, while a low debt/equity ratio of 0.32 and a current ratio of 1.42 point to a conservatively financed balance sheet. The reported gross margin of nearly 63% looks high but compresses sharply to a 16.7% operating margin and 12.4% net margin, which is the more meaningful read on profitability.

The clear drag is Growth, scoring just 19.6. Revenue rose only 0.86% year-over-year, and although EPS grew 9%, the top line is essentially flat — a reminder that this is a mature, commodity-linked business whose fortunes track oil prices more than organic expansion.

A reader should be cautious about leaning on the momentum score: energy momentum is cyclical and can reverse quickly with crude prices, so a high reading late in a run warrants scrutiny of where oil sits. The "cheap" value signal may simply reflect the market pricing in that cyclicality. Note too that several diagnostics — Debt/EBITDA, Altman Z, Piotroski F-score — are unavailable, leaving gaps in the leverage and quality picture worth verifying independently.

M.text:
Macy's lands at #18 primarily on the strength of its Value factor, which sits at an exceptional 92.7. The valuation metrics justify this: a P/E of 9.04, P/B of just 1.04, P/S of 0.27, and a strikingly low P/FCF of 4.89. On price alone, the market is assigning very little premium to the business. Momentum is middling at 58.9, while Quality (39.4) and Growth (39.9) drag against the value story. The tension here is that a value score this high usually reflects a market that expects little. Revenue growth is essentially flat (-0.35%), which explains the weak Growth score, while thin margins — 4.19% operating and just 2.94% net — mean profitability is fragile and sensitive to any pressure on sales or costs. The eye-popping 22.94% EPS growth, 39.1% FCF growth, and 392% earnings surprise deserve scrutiny: such figures often reflect a low prior-year base or one-off items rather than durable improvement.

A reader should check whether the recent earnings surprise and FCF jump are repeatable or cyclical, and weigh the retail sector's structural challenges against the cheap multiple. Debt looks manageable (D/E 0.5, Debt/EBITDA 1.26, current ratio 1.48), but the modest Quality and Growth scores suggest the cheapness may be pricing in stagnation rather than a bargain.

OFG.text:
OFG Bancorp lands at #19 with a final score of 57.1, and the ranking is carried primarily by its Value and Quality factors. On value, the stock screens cheaply: a P/E of roughly 10, P/B of 1.25, and P/FCF near 11 place it in the 76th percentile, reflecting the modest multiples typical of regional banks. Quality (67.4) is backed by solid profitability — ROE of 15.6% and ROIC of 14.7% are respectable for the sector, alongside a healthy 26.9% net margin and 39.2% operating margin. Revenue growth of 28% year-over-year and a 25% earnings surprise show recent operating strength.

The weaker factors temper the picture. Momentum sits at just 34, suggesting the share price has lagged even as fundamentals held up — worth checking whether the market is discounting something the trailing numbers don't capture. Growth (47) is middling: EPS grew a more modest 16% against the 28% revenue figure, and FCF actually declined 13.8%, a divergence a reader should reconcile against the headline top-line growth.

Note that many bank-specific gauges here read "n/a" — gross margin, current ratio, Altman Z and Piotroski scores — so the Quality read leans heavily on profitability ratios. For a bank, credit quality, deposit trends, and net interest margin sensitivity are not visible in these metrics and warrant separate review.

NTB.text:
Butterfield's #2 ranking (70.1/100) is anchored by its Quality score of 80.8 and Value score of 75.6, a rare combination that reflects a genuinely profitable business trading at an undemanding price. Profitability is the standout: ROE of 21.63% and ROIC of 21.01% are strong for a bank, and net and operating margins near 40% show the business converts a large share of revenue into profit. On valuation, a P/E of 10.1 and P/FCF of 9.74 are modest, while the 1.85 P/B is reasonable given the high returns on equity. Low reported debt/equity of 0.12 rounds out a clean-looking balance sheet, and the recent 8.2% earnings surprise supports the picture. Growth (61.7) and Momentum (58.3) are middling but not weak, with headline revenue growth of 47.41% and EPS growth of 19.85%.

A few things warrant a closer look. Standard bank-specific caveats apply: gross margin, current ratio, Altman Z and Piotroski aren't computed here (typical for financials), so the "clean" leverage reading understates a bank's real balance-sheet complexity — deposits, loan quality and interest-rate exposure aren't captured by debt/equity. The 47% revenue growth also looks unusually high and may partly reflect the interest-rate environment rather than organic expansion; check whether net interest margin is peaking. Finally, Momentum being the weakest factor suggests price action lags the fundamentals — worth confirming whether that reflects sector-wide caution on banks rather than a company-specific issue.

INSW.text:
International Seaways tops the ranked universe largely on the strength of its Momentum score (96.6), which is by far its standout factor. That's reinforced by a striking 47.6% earnings surprise and 69.8% year-over-year EPS growth, signals that the tanker market has been running hot in its favor. Quality is also solid at 74.8, backed by genuinely impressive profitability: 27.1% ROE, 20.7% ROIC, and net margins above 55%. The balance sheet looks conservative too, with debt/equity of 0.27, debt/EBITDA of 1.16, a current ratio of 7.34, and an Altman Z-Score of 5.19 that suggests low bankruptcy risk. A Piotroski score of 7/9 rounds out a financially healthy picture. Value (55.6) and Growth (56.6) are middling — the 7.85 P/E looks cheap on the surface, but that's typical for cyclical shipping names.

The main thing to scrutinize is the cyclicality behind these numbers. Shipping companies post enormous margins and low P/Es at the top of freight-rate cycles, and a single-digit P/E often reflects the market pricing in an eventual downturn rather than a bargain. The 96.6 Momentum score, paired with a 47% earnings beat, may indicate this stock is late in a strong run rather than early. Note also that despite 14.5% revenue growth, free cash flow actually fell 11.8% year-over-year, and P/FCF of 31 is far less flattering than the trailing P/E. Worth checking whether current earnings and day rates are sustainable or peak-cycle figures.

ASB.text:
Associated Banc-Corp's #13 ranking and 61.5 composite are driven primarily by its Value and Growth factors, both sitting in the low-80s percentiles. On valuation, the stock trades at a P/E of 10.27, a P/S of 2.01, and notably a price-to-book of 0.86 — below the value of its net assets, which is common for regional banks the market views cautiously. The Growth score is inflated by eye-catching year-over-year figures: 90.85% revenue growth and 217.9% EPS growth, alongside a modest 1.88% earnings surprise. Quality is middling at 50.9, consistent with a 10.04% ROE, 8.5% ROIC, and healthy reported net (28.74%) and operating (35.92%) margins. Leverage looks conservative at a 0.2 debt/equity ratio, and there are no penalties.

The main thing to scrutinize is the growth data. Triple-digit EPS growth off a bank almost always reflects a depressed prior-year base — one-off charges, provisioning swings, or securities losses in the comparison period — rather than sustainable expansion; note FCF growth was only 6.1%, a far more sober number. The sub-1.0 P/B "cheapness" also deserves context: banks trade below book when investors doubt asset quality, deposit stability, or net-interest-margin durability, so a reader should check credit provisions, deposit trends and unrealized bond losses. Finally, the weak Momentum score (35.4) signals the market has not rewarded these results with price strength, pulling against the strong Value and Growth signals — worth reconciling before drawing conclusions.

AUB.text:
Atlantic Union Bankshares lands at #26 with a 55.5 composite, and the ranking is led by its Value score (69.8), backed up by cheap-looking multiples: a P/B right at 1.0, a P/E of 17.4, and a strikingly low P/FCF of 2.63. Growth is the second contributor (62.4), reflecting eye-catching top-line figures — revenue up 48% year-over-year and free cash flow up over 600%. Quality is middling at 51.8, and Momentum is the weakest factor at 40.1, suggesting the stock's price trend has lagged the broader ranked universe even as the fundamentals screen cheap. Balance-sheet leverage looks modest for a bank, with debt/equity at 0.18, and reported operating and net margins (36% and 30%) are healthy on the surface.

The numbers warrant several caveats. The headline revenue and FCF growth almost certainly reflect acquisition activity or accounting effects rather than pure organic expansion — note that EPS grew only 6.7% over the same period, a large gap that hints the growth isn't flowing to per-share earnings. Profitability is the soft spot: ROE of 6.99% and ROIC of 5.93% are low, which likely explains why a P/B of 1.0 isn't as much of a bargain as it appears — the market is pricing modest returns on the equity base. A reader should also weigh the weak Momentum score, which can signal the market disagrees with the value case, and check how much of that 30% net margin depends on net interest income sensitive to rate moves.

DHT.text:
DHT Holdings lands at #4 with a 68.5 score, and the ranking is anchored by an exceptional Quality reading of 82.7. The underlying profitability metrics justify that: ROE of 29.1% and ROIC of 21.9% are strong, while gross, operating and net margins of roughly 66%, 61% and 59% are unusually fat — a signature of the crude tanker business when charter rates are elevated. Leverage looks contained, with debt/equity at 0.41 and a current ratio of 1.83. Growth (54.7) is the weakest leg, held back by revenue growth of just 4.2% even as EPS jumped 85.8%.

The tension here is worth scrutinizing. That EPS surge against nearly flat revenue points to cyclical margin expansion — tanker day-rates — rather than a growing top line, so the 8.6x P/E may reflect peak-cycle earnings that don't persist. The gap between the low P/E and the higher P/FCF (18.8x) also hints that reported net income is running ahead of actual cash generation. Several diagnostics — Debt/EBITDA, Altman Z, Piotroski F — are unavailable, limiting the leverage and quality cross-check. A reader should verify where spot rates sit relative to history and how much of the momentum reflects a mature move rather than a fresh one.

MD.text:
Pediatrix lands at #28 on the strength of its Value and Momentum scores, both hovering near 79. The valuation case is concrete: a P/E of 12.5, P/S of 1.13, and an especially cheap P/FCF of 5.84 suggest the market is paying little for the group's cash generation. Momentum is reinforced by fundamental progress rather than just price — EPS grew nearly 35% year-over-year, free cash flow jumped 31%, and the most recent earnings beat came in at 12.9%. Quality sits mid-pack at 54, but the underlying profitability metrics are solid: 20% ROE, ~12% ROIC, and a strong Piotroski F-Score of 8/9 point to a well-run, improving operation. Net margin of 9% and operating margin of 12.4% are respectable for a physician-services business.

The weak spots temper the picture. Growth scores just 43, dragged down by revenue that actually shrank 2.25% year-over-year — meaning the impressive EPS and FCF gains are coming from cost control, buybacks, or divestitures rather than top-line expansion, which is worth verifying for durability. The model also applies a -10 penalty for an Altman Z-Score of 2.21, which falls in the "grey zone" and flags some balance-sheet stress; Debt/EBITDA of 2.47 and Debt/Equity of 0.67 confirm meaningful leverage. A reader should check whether the earnings momentum is sustainable without revenue growth, and whether the leverage and thin liquidity (current ratio 1.33) leave much cushion if margins compress.

THG.text:
Hanover Insurance lands at #8 largely on the strength of its Value factor (83.3), the standout of its four scores. The valuation metrics back that up: a P/E of 10.49, P/S of 1.13, P/B of 1.71, and a particularly low P/FCF of 6.06 all point to a business priced modestly relative to earnings and cash generation. Quality is respectable at 61.5, supported by a solid 20.92% ROE and 16.1% ROIC, plus conservative leverage — Debt/Equity of just 0.24 and Debt/EBITDA of 1.31 leave the balance sheet in comfortable shape. Insurance earnings are notoriously lumpy, so the 24% earnings surprise and outsized EPS growth may reflect a benign loss year rather than a durable step-change; a reader should check whether those tailwinds are repeatable.

Also worth noting: the Piotroski F-Score of 6/9 is decent but not exceptional, and net margin of 10.8% is thin in absolute terms, typical for a P&C insurer exposed to catastrophe volatility. The cheap valuation partly reflects that cyclicality — verify whether recent profitability is normal or peak.

EVR.text:
Evercore's #15 ranking (59.4/100) is anchored by a strong Quality score of 86.6, which the fundamentals support convincingly. The advisory firm posts an ROE of 41% and ROIC of 32%, indicating it generates substantial returns on capital without leaning on debt — Debt/Equity sits at a modest 0.3 and the current ratio of 2.77 points to comfortable liquidity. Growth (74.5) is the other pillar: revenue climbed 47.3% year-over-year and EPS jumped 69.8%, capped by a 46.7% earnings surprise, all consistent with a cyclical rebound in dealmaking and capital-markets activity. Value is middling at 56.8; a P/E of 17.2 and P/FCF of 7.3 look reasonable, though the P/B of 7.03 reflects an asset-light business where book value understates the franchise.

The clear drag is Momentum at 17.4, a bottom-decile reading that pulls against the otherwise upbeat picture. That divergence is worth scrutinizing: strong trailing growth and a large earnings beat have not translated into price strength, which can signal that the market is either skeptical the growth is durable or already anticipating a slowdown.

A reader should remember that advisory revenue is highly cyclical and lumpy — the 47% growth and 47% surprise are measured off a weak comparison period, so year-over-year figures may flatter the trend. The 99% "gross margin" is a services-accounting artifact; the more telling 22% operating and 16% net margins reflect heavy compensation costs. Missing Piotroski and Altman scores also leave some quality signals unverified.

BAP.text:

A few things warrant a closer look. The strong momentum score comes after a meaningful run, so a reader should consider how much of the good news is already reflected in a price near $389 and a P/B of 2.29, which is toward the richer end for a bank. The heavy insider selling sits awkwardly against that strength and deserves scrutiny — it can reflect routine diversification or something more. Note also that many balance-sheet and safety metrics (Altman Z, Piotroski, current ratio, Debt/EBITDA) are unavailable because standard formulas don't map cleanly to banks; Debt/Equity of 0.77 and ROIC of 10.2% are the visible leverage and efficiency signals worth verifying against peer banks.

FCF.text:

Readers should scrutinize the gap between that 56.91% revenue growth and the much slower 12.41% EPS growth, which suggests rising costs, provisioning, or share dilution eating into the top line. The -8.57% latest earnings surprise reinforces that the recent quarter fell short of expectations, and may explain the weak momentum. Verify whether loan growth and credit quality justify the revenue surge.

BOH.text:
Bank of Hawaii's #35 rank and 52.8 score rest largely on its Growth (67.4) and Quality (58.1) scores. The growth figures stand out: revenue and EPS both up roughly 38.5% year-over-year, with FCF growth of 14.3%. A reader should weigh that weakness against the strong growth score, and question how durable that 38% revenue and EPS growth is — such rates are often partly cyclical (net interest margin swings, comparison against a depressed prior year) rather than a sustainable run-rate. The latest earnings surprise was negative at -3.27%, a modest miss worth noting against the growth narrative. ROE (12.1%) and ROIC (11.7%) are respectable but not exceptional. Bank fundamentals also hinge on credit quality, deposit costs, and loan-book exposure — items this factor model doesn't capture and worth checking directly.

WBS.text:

On valuation, the stock trades at a P/E of 12.06 and, notably, a P/B of 1.17 — modest for a bank and the main reason Value scores 71.6. FCF growth is actually negative (-26.3%), diverging sharply from the reported EPS gains, which is worth reconciling. Standard leverage and liquidity ratios (current ratio, Altman Z, gross margin) are "n/a" because banking-sector accounting differs; the low D/E understates a bank's true balance-sheet leverage. Finally, the pedestrian Momentum score means the strong fundamentals aren't being confirmed by price action.

IFS.text:

Value scores highest at 85.2, backed by a P/E of just 6.67, a P/FCF near 7.8 and a P/B of 1.53 — inexpensive multiples for a bank posting a 29.68% ROE. Quality is the softer factor at 58.3; the 17.6% net margin and 13.91% ROIC are respectable but not exceptional, and Debt/Equity of 1.11 reflects the leverage inherent to a financial-services model.

The most concrete flag is the -15 penalty for insiders selling far more than they bought — worth checking against a stock that has clearly rerated recently, since a strong momentum score late in a run can coincide with management taking money off the table. The explosive EPS growth (126%) is also worth scrutinizing: such a figure often reflects a low prior-year base or one-off items rather than a sustainable run-rate, so the 29% revenue growth is the steadier gauge. Note too that many bank-specific quality checks (Piotroski, Altman Z, gross margin, current ratio) show as n/a, meaning the Quality read leans heavily on ROE and margins. Readers may want to examine loan-book quality, provisioning and currency exposure behind the headline numbers.

MOG.B.text:

Growth reinforces this at 71.5, backed by real operating improvement: revenue up 16% year-over-year, EPS up 49%, and free cash flow up a striking 282%. An 8.45% earnings surprise and a solid Piotroski F-Score of 7/9 suggest the recent operational trajectory is genuine rather than cosmetic. Readers should weigh how much of the score is a momentum run that has already happened versus durable fundamentals. A 40x earnings multiple leaves little room for a growth stumble, and the modest returns on capital mean the premium rests on continued execution. Leverage is reasonable (Debt/EBITDA 1.71, Z-Score 5.63), so balance-sheet risk is not the primary concern here.

CUBI.text:
